clinician.trajectory_summary: A 41-year-old unvaccinated male presented with a 3-day history of worsening headache, nausea, and photophobia. On admission, he was alert with normal vital signs and no meningeal signs on initial neurological examination. Initial blood tests and head CT were unremarkable. However, on closer examination, vesicular rash with blisters were observed on the left side of his nose and hard palate in the distribution of the second branch of the trigeminal nerve (V2), consistent with herpes zoster ophthalmicus. The patient reported preceding skin rashes and oral dysesthesia before the onset of meningitis symptoms. Lumbar puncture revealed cerebrospinal fluid with lymphocytic pleocytosis (217/μL with 92% lymphocytes), elevated protein (129 mg/dL), and low glucose (55 mg/dL relative to blood glucose of 138 mg/dL), consistent with viral meningitis. The clinical presentation of meningitis symptoms combined with dermatomal vesicular rash in the trigeminal nerve distribution, along with the characteristic CSF profile, strongly supported VZV meningitis. The patient was treated with intravenous acyclovir for 14 days, resulting in improvement of symptoms.
